questiontext.text: Which C++ keyword enables runtime (dynamic) polymorphism on a member function?

feedback.text: Correct — declaring a function virtual enables dynamic dispatch.
No — static binds at compile time, the opposite of dynamic dispatch.
No — inline is only a hint about function expansion.
No — friend grants access, it has nothing to do with dispatch.

generalfeedback.text: Runtime polymorphism in C++ relies on virtual member functions resolved through the vtable.

questiontext.text: A Base* pointer actually points to a Derived object and calls a virtual function. Which implementation runs?

answer.text: The Derived class's override, selected at run time

feedback.text: Correct — dynamic dispatch picks the most-derived override.

answer.text: The Base class's version, chosen from the pointer type

feedback.text: No — with virtual functions the dynamic type decides.

answer.text: Neither; the call is ambiguous and fails to compile

feedback.text: No — this is exactly the case virtual functions handle.
No — only the resolved override runs (unless it explicitly calls Base).

generalfeedback.text: Through a base pointer/reference, a virtual call dispatches to the override belonging to the object's dynamic type.

questiontext.text: When is a virtual function call resolved to a concrete implementation?

answer.text: At run time, via the object's vtable

feedback.text: Correct — that is dynamic dispatch.

answer.text: At compile time, from the static pointer type

feedback.text: No — that would be static (early) binding.

answer.text: At link time, by the linker

feedback.text: No — the linker does not choose virtual overrides per call.

answer.text: Never; virtual calls are forbidden through pointers

feedback.text: No — pointers/references are exactly how they are used.

generalfeedback.text: Virtual calls use late (dynamic) binding: the vtable is consulted at run time to find the correct override.

feedback.text: Correct — a common base interface, many derived behaviors.
No — that is closer to aliasing, not polymorphism.
No — polymorphism depends on a shared interface.
No — that describes static, not runtime, polymorphism.

generalfeedback.text: Runtime polymorphism gives one interface (the base class) with many implementations (the overrides).

questiontext.text: Which statements about C++ runtime polymorphism are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: It requires functions declared virtual in the base class

feedback.text: Yes — virtual is the trigger for dynamic dispatch.

answer.text: Dispatch is resolved at run time through the vtable

feedback.text: Yes — the object's dynamic type is consulted at run time.

answer.text: It is resolved entirely at compile time by overload resolution

feedback.text: No — that describes ad-hoc (overloading) polymorphism.

answer.text: It works through a base pointer only if the function is non-virtual

feedback.text: No — a non-virtual function binds to the static type, defeating dispatch.

generalfeedback.text: Runtime polymorphism needs virtual functions and dispatches via the vtable at run time; non-virtual calls bind statically.

questiontext.text: Calling a virtual function through a base-class pointer invokes the derived class's override.

feedback.text: Correct — the dynamic type of the object determines which override runs.
With virtual functions the derived override is indeed selected.

questiontext.text: A non-virtual member function called through a base pointer is dispatched dynamically to the derived version.

feedback.text: No — without virtual the call binds to the static (pointer) type.
Correct — non-virtual calls use static binding, not dynamic dispatch.

questiontext.text: The C++ keyword that marks a member function for dynamic dispatch is ______.

feedback.text: Correct — the virtual keyword.
Correct.
